issues.note: A very thin Sunday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 7 picks rather than padding. The EM items are an open-fracture antibiotic timing meta-analysis, sepsis fluid balance trajectories, frailty and mortality after stroke lytics, and adjunctive nicorandil with STEMI fibrinolysis. A drug anaphylaxis risk-factor study, a UK ICU stewardship audit and a CYP2C19/PPI cohort round it out; all are observational.
bottom_line: Pooled data couldn't confirm a safe time window for antibiotics after open fractures, but the four studies with validated infection definitions saw about 4-fold higher deep infection odds with delay. Keep cefazolin going in as early as possible.

Septic ICU patients who kept accumulating fluid on days 3–7 had about 30% higher adjusted odds of dying by day 28 (observational). Once resuscitation is done, stop reflexive maintenance fluids in boarding sepsis patients and concentrate drips.
In UK ICUs, a pre-set stop or review date on an antimicrobial order made a 72-hour review about 9 times more likely. It's an easy field to build into ED antibiotic order sets.

articles.takeaway: Antibiotic delay after open fracture wasn't clearly tied to deep infection overall, but rigorous studies saw about 4x higher odds
articles.title: Time From Injury to First Antibiotic Administration and Deep Infection Risk in Open Fractures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.population: 24 observational studies of open fractures; 16 pooled (5,283 patients, 508 deep infections)
articles.summary: The authors kept time-from-injury and time-from-arrival studies in separate analyses because they measure different exposures. Neither stratum showed a significant link between delay and deep infection (injury-anchored OR 1.62, 95% CI 0.87–3.00; arrival-anchored OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.86–2.07), and no time cutoff could be estimated. The split between studies tracked how infection was defined: the 4 studies using a validated definition found OR 4.34 with delay, while 7 using an operative proxy found no effect (OR 0.86). That subgroup finding was post hoc and confounded, and overall certainty was very low.
articles.why: Absence of evidence isn't permission to wait. Keep weight-based cefazolin (2 g, 3 g if 120 kg or more) stocked in the trauma bay or automated cabinet so it goes in within the first hour, and document the injury time so delays can be audited.

articles.takeaway: Septic ICU patients who kept gaining fluid on days 3–7 had about 30% higher odds of 28-day death
articles.title: Association Between Daily Fluid Balance Trajectories and Dynamic Organ Failure Resolution (SOFA-2) in Sepsis: A Latent Class Growth Analysis of 16 262 Patients.
articles.population: 16,262 adults with sepsis who survived at least 72 hours in the ICU, MIMIC-IV database (US)
articles.summary: Daily net fluid balance from ICU day 3 to day 7 sorted patients into three patterns: steady low balance (85%), delayed decline after day 5 (8%) and continuous accumulation (6%). The steady group had the lowest 28-day mortality (20.8%) and the fastest SOFA-2 recovery. After adjusting for illness severity, loop diuretics and dialysis, the delayed group (aOR 1.30) and the accumulating group (aOR 1.27) had higher mortality. The authors treat the trajectories as markers of how sick the patient is, not proof that fluid itself causes harm.
articles.why: Fluid is a drug with a cumulative dose. For long ED boarders, pharmacists can flag maintenance fluids that keep running after resuscitation, concentrate antibiotic and vasopressor drips, and prompt a daily fluid balance check.

articles.takeaway: Frailty predicted 1-year death after IV lytics in older stroke patients, but it isn't a reason to withhold treatment
articles.title: Hospital frailty risk score and one-year mortality after intravenous thrombolysis in older patients with acute ischemic stroke.
articles.population: 423 adults aged 65 or older given IV thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, 1 center, 2014–2019
articles.summary: About 15% of patients had an elevated Hospital Frailty Risk Score (5 or more). One-year mortality was 34.9% in that group vs 20.6% in the low-risk group, and each additional point raised the hazard of death by about 8.5% after adjusting for age, comorbidity, NIHSS and ASPECTS (HR 1.085). Adding the score improved the prognostic model. The authors stress that the findings don't support withholding reperfusion.
articles.why: Frail older patients still benefit from tenecteplase or alteplase, so this belongs in goals-of-care and discharge planning, not the go/no-go decision. Pharmacists should still use an accurate weight for dosing and review antithrombotic plans before discharge.

articles.takeaway: Adding nicorandil to pro-urokinase lysis for STEMI was linked to better reperfusion and fewer 30-day MACE
articles.title: Adjunctive Nicorandil Ameliorates Cardiac Function and Clinical Outcomes Following Recombinant Human Pro-Urokinase Thrombolysis in Patients With Acute ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction.
articles.population: 116 adults with STEMI given IV recombinant pro-urokinase (62 with nicorandil, 54 without), China, 2024–2026
articles.summary: Successful reperfusion was 79% with nicorandil vs 61% without, and ST-segment resolution at 2 hours was 74% vs 56%. The nicorandil group also had lower troponin I and CK-MB at 24 hours, better ejection fraction and smaller LV diameter on day 7, and fewer serious arrhythmias and 30-day MACE. Adverse drug reactions were similar. Treatment wasn't randomized and the sample was small.
articles.why: Neither nicorandil nor pro-urokinase is available in the US, so this is hypothesis-generating. For US EDs without timely PCI, tenecteplase (weight-based, max 50 mg) plus aspirin, clopidogrel and an anticoagulant remains the regimen to have ready.

articles.takeaway: Asthma, NERD, food allergy and suspected beta-lactam allergy marked adults with a history of drug anaphylaxis
articles.title: Clinical patterns of suspected drug hypersensitivity and factors associated with drug-related anaphylaxis: a real-world study of 1,037 adults.
articles.population: 1,037 adults referred to a tertiary allergy clinic for suspected drug hypersensitivity, 2022–2023
articles.summary: NSAIDs (61%) and antibiotics (51%) were the most commonly suspected culprits, with beta-lactams named by 42% of patients. Urticaria, angioedema and bronchospasm were the most common reactions, and 25% reported drug-related anaphylaxis. Asthma (aOR 1.64), NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease (aOR 2.79), food allergy (aOR 2.76) and suspected beta-lactam hypersensitivity (aOR 1.81) were independently associated with an anaphylaxis history. It's a referred population, so the associations can't show cause.
articles.why: When an ED patient reports an NSAID or beta-lactam allergy, these comorbidities help separate a likely serious reaction from a low-risk label. Take a specific reaction history, keep IM epinephrine (0.5 mg) ready, and refer low-risk penicillin labels for delabeling.

articles.takeaway: Three-quarters of empiric ICU antibiotic orders followed local guidance; a set review date made 72-hour review 9x likelier
articles.title: Antimicrobial stewardship and resistance in intensive care units in the UK: a prospective national audit.
articles.population: 2,626 adults in 154 UK ICUs (point-prevalence survey with longitudinal follow-up)
articles.summary: Antimicrobials were prescribed to 61% of ICU patients. Of 2,116 empiric orders, 75% followed unit guidelines; 12% deviated after discussion with infection specialists, and 9.5% deviated with no justification or discussion. Review within 72 hours happened for 93% of eligible orders, and a pre-specified stop or review date was the strongest predictor of that review (adjusted OR 9.3, 95% CI 5.4–16.2).
articles.why: Antibiotics started in the ED often run unreviewed through a long boarding stay. A required stop or review date field in ED order sets is a low-effort, pharmacist-owned stewardship fix.

articles.takeaway: CYP2C19 metabolizer status wasn't linked to recurrent GERD documentation after starting a PPI
articles.title: CYP2C19 metabolizer phenotype and recurrent documented gastroesophageal reflux disease after proton pump inhibitor initiation: A cohort study from the All of Us Research Program.
articles.population: 21,135 adults with GERD, a definitive CYP2C19 phenotype and 1 year of follow-up after PPI start, All of Us Research Program
articles.summary: Recurrent GERD documentation in the following year occurred in 28%. Compared with normal metabolizers, adjusted risk ratios were 1.11 for poor, 1.02 for intermediate, 1.04 for rapid and 0.97 for ultrarapid metabolizers, none significant, and results held when limited to omeprazole. Further reflux testing or procedures were rare (1.2%) and also unrelated to phenotype. PPI dose and ongoing use weren't modeled.
articles.why: The authors say this doesn't overturn CPIC's advice to raise PPI doses in rapid and ultrarapid metabolizers. In the ED, CYP2C19 status matters more for clopidogrel choice after ACS than for a discharge PPI.

issues.note: A thin Saturday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs 8 picks. The EM items are a point-of-care DOAC level test validated in two EDs, a clinician review of semaglutide overdose, real-world low-dose alteplase decisions in stroke and a large pediatric ED influenza antiviral comparison. An opioid-free anesthesia RCT, a ceftazidime-avibactam combination meta-analysis, ampicillin-sulbactam hypokalemia and an HFpEF drug-class network meta-analysis round it out.
bottom_line: A whole-blood point-of-care test measured apixaban and rivaroxaban levels in a median of 14 minutes vs 73 for the lab anti-Xa assay, with strong agreement at the 50 and 100 ng/mL reversal and surgery thresholds. It could speed andexanet or 4F-PCC decisions once it's available.

Semaglutide overdose mostly means days to weeks of vomiting, dehydration and AKI because of its roughly 1-week half-life; there's no antidote and dialysis doesn't help. Hypoglycemia is the exception, mainly with insulin, sulfonylureas or counterfeit pens.
About 1 in 5 inpatients on ampicillin-sulbactam became hypokalemic, at a median of day 4. Recheck potassium around days 4–5 in patients over 75 or starting at 3.9 mEq/L or below.

articles.takeaway: A bedside test measured apixaban and rivaroxaban levels about an hour faster than the lab, with close agreement
articles.title: A bicentric pilot study of apixaban and rivaroxaban quantification using a novel point-of-care system in the emergency department.
articles.population: 69 DOAC-treated ED patients with paired samples, 2 EDs, plus a preliminary lab validation
articles.summary: Paired whole-blood point-of-care results were compared with a standard lab anti-Xa assay calibrated for each drug. In the ED cohort, correlation was 0.965 with a slope near 1 and a median bias of about −10 ng/mL. Agreement at clinical cutoffs improved as thresholds rose (kappa 0.62 at 30, 0.89 at 50 and 0.94 at 100 ng/mL), and precision was acceptable (CV under 6%). Median time to result was 14 minutes vs 73 minutes for the lab.
articles.why: Guidance often uses about 50 ng/mL (bleeding) or 30 ng/mL (urgent surgery) to decide on andexanet or 4F-PCC. A 15-minute level could prevent unneeded reversal in patients whose last dose was long ago; agreement was weakest at 30 ng/mL, so confirm low results before surgery.

articles.takeaway: Semaglutide overdose causes prolonged vomiting and dehydration; care is supportive and observation should respect its long half-life
articles.title: Recognition and management of semaglutide overdose and intoxication: a narrative review for clinicians.
articles.population: Literature through July 2026: trials, case reports, case series and poison center and pharmacovigilance data on semaglutide excess exposure
articles.summary: Most overdoses come from dosing errors, unit confusion with compounded multi-dose vials and products bought outside regulated supply. The main syndrome is gastrointestinal and protracted (nausea, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia) because the half-life is close to a week, and volume loss, electrolyte problems and AKI drive serious outcomes. Isolated overdose rarely causes hypoglycemia, but it does occur with insulin or sulfonylureas, in people without diabetes and with insulin-containing counterfeit pens. Pancreatitis, euglycemic ketoacidosis, ileus and aspiration from delayed gastric emptying are less common but dangerous.
articles.why: Expect more of these as compounded semaglutide spreads: confirm the product and units (mg vs mL vs "units"), give aggressive antiemetics, fluids and electrolytes, check glucose based on co-medications, and use full-stomach precautions for sedation or RSI. Poison center input helps set the observation period.

articles.takeaway: Lower alteplase doses went to older, diabetic patients; worse outcomes reflected who got them, not the dose itself
articles.title: Clinician-Selected Alteplase Dosing in Acute Ischemic Stroke: Treatment Patterns and Adjusted Outcomes in a Taiwanese Registry.
articles.population: 418 adults with acute ischemic stroke given IV alteplase without thrombectomy, Taiwan, 2017–2022
articles.summary: Doses were grouped as low (0.46–0.64 mg/kg), medium (0.67–0.84) or standard (0.85–0.94). Each year of age raised the odds of a low dose (aOR 1.07), and diabetes was linked to medium (aOR 1.84) and low (aOR 2.71) doses. Good 90-day function (mRS 0–2) was 44%, 54% and 68% across low, medium and standard groups, but dose category wasn't independently associated with outcome after adjustment. Symptomatic ICH was too rare to compare.
articles.why: Low-dose alteplase (0.6 mg/kg) is still used in Asia, but this doesn't show it's safer or equivalent, and ENCHANTED didn't show noninferiority. Standard dosing (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg) or tenecteplase remains the default; pharmacists should use a measured or best-estimate weight rather than rounding down.

articles.takeaway: Baloxavir and peramivir cleared fever about half a day faster than oseltamivir in children seen in a pediatric ED
articles.title: Clinical features and comparative outcomes of antiviral treatment in children with influenza A and B: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
articles.population: 3,718 children with confirmed influenza A (1,717) or B (2,001) treated within 48 hours of fever, 1 tertiary pediatric ED in China, 2023–2024 season
articles.summary: After matching within each influenza type, fever resolved faster with baloxavir (about 1.5 vs 2.1–2.3 days) and peramivir (about 1.7 vs 2.2 days) than with oseltamivir. Differences in full symptom resolution were smaller and inconsistent. Recorded adverse events were 16.5% with oseltamivir vs 5.0% with peramivir and 3.6% with baloxavir, with no serious events. Influenza A brought more high fever and neurologic complications, and influenza B more GI symptoms.
articles.why: Relevant as flu season ramps up: single-dose baloxavir (approved in the US for ages 5 and up) avoids a 5-day oseltamivir course and its vomiting. Oseltamivir is still preferred for hospitalized, severely ill or very young children, and in pregnancy.

articles.takeaway: Dexmedetomidine-esketamine anesthesia slightly improved recovery scores, with less hypotension and nausea than sufentanil
articles.title: Opioid-free vs. opioid-inclusive anaesthesia in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multicentre randomised controlled trial.
articles.population: 315 adults having elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, multicenter in China, 2025
articles.summary: Patients got opioid-free anesthesia (dexmedetomidine, esketamine and sevoflurane) or sufentanil plus sevoflurane, with NSAID and wound infiltration in both arms. The 24-hour overall benefit of analgesia score was better with opioid-free anesthesia (adjusted difference −1.3 points), but that was short of the 3-point clinically important threshold. Pain on movement and chronic pain at 90 days (16% vs 16%) didn't differ. Intraoperative hypotension (20% vs 36%) and postoperative nausea and vomiting (23% vs 34%) were less common without opioids.
articles.why: Supports ketamine-plus-alpha-2 agonist combinations as an option when you want to avoid opioid nausea or hypotension, but not as an across-the-board replacement. The same agents show up in ED analgesia and sedation, where subdissociative ketamine is already an opioid-sparing choice.

articles.takeaway: Adding a second drug to ceftazidime-avibactam didn't lower mortality in carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections
articles.title: Ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy versus combination therapy for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections: a secondary meta-analysis of predominantly critically ill cohorts.
articles.population: 25 cohort studies, 2,676 adults with carbapenem-resistant gram-negative infections (about 82% in the ICU)
articles.summary: This reanalysis of an existing dataset found 30-day mortality of 31.2% with combination therapy vs 32.8% with monotherapy (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.79–1.04). Clinical cure, AKI and on-treatment resistance didn't differ significantly, and microbiological eradication was borderline (RR 1.15, p = 0.05). Polymyxin-containing combinations trended toward more nephrotoxicity (RR 1.28, not significant). All included studies were observational, so certainty is very low.
articles.why: Supports ceftazidime-avibactam monotherapy as a reasonable default for KPC-type infections, sparing patients polymyxin or aminoglycoside toxicity. Combinations may still make sense for MBL producers (with aztreonam) or very high-risk sources.

articles.takeaway: About 1 in 5 patients on ampicillin-sulbactam developed hypokalemia, usually around day 4
articles.title: Incidence of and Factors Associated with Hypokalemia During Sulbactam/Ampicillin Therapy: A Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.population: 182 hospitalized adults with normal potassium at the start of more than 2 days of ampicillin-sulbactam, 1 Japanese hospital, 2022–2024
articles.summary: Hypokalemia developed in 39 patients (21.4%), and 6 fell to 3.0 mEq/L or lower. Median time to onset was 4 days (range 2–13). A decision-tree analysis identified baseline potassium of 3.9 mEq/L or lower and age over 75 as the factors associated with hypokalemia. It is a small single-center study without outcome data.
articles.why: High-dose penicillins act as nonreabsorbable anions that increase renal potassium loss. For older patients started on ampicillin-sulbactam in the ED for aspiration pneumonia or skin infections, schedule a potassium recheck around days 4–5, especially with diuretics or low-normal baseline levels.

articles.takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors and MRAs gave the most reliable benefit in HF with EF over 40%; no class lowered mortality
articles.title: Incremental associations of pharmacological components in heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction: a systematic review and component network meta-analysis.
articles.population: 24 phase 3/4 RCTs in HFmrEF/HFpEF (LVEF over 40%); primary network of 10 trials and 12 regimens
articles.summary: For cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization, incretin-based drugs (semaglutide or tirzepatide; HR 0.69), SGLT2 inhibitors (0.80), ARNIs (0.82) and MRAs (0.89) each showed incremental benefit, mostly from fewer hospitalizations. No class significantly reduced mortality. SGLT2 inhibitors and MRAs held up across most sensitivity analyses, while ARNI and incretin results were sensitive to trial selection and low certainty.
articles.why: Supports an SGLT2 inhibitor as the foundation, with an MRA added when potassium and renal function allow, for HFpEF patients admitted or discharged from the ED. Watch for MRA-related hyperkalemia in patients who come back with AKI.

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window, so the 8 picks lean on toxicology. Clinical Toxicology published three ED-relevant cohorts (naloxone infusions, massive GHB exposures, and kratom/phenibut/tianeptine), alongside a stroke meta-analysis on IV lytics before thrombectomy, a review of why sepsis steroid meta-analyses disagree, and ED opioid prescribing trends. An AJHP diagnostic stewardship study and an ICU infection-prevention meta-analysis fill out the rest.
bottom_line: About 1 in 5 ED opioid overdoses got a naloxone infusion, and fentanyl or opioid-plus-stimulant exposure tripled the odds. Long runs of dilute infusions added a lot of IV fluid, so concentrate the bag and reassess often.

In 154 massive GHB exposures, 75% arrived with a GCS of 3 and two-thirds were intubated, yet only 1 died and 27% went home straight from the ED. Supportive care works; an opioid on board raised the odds of hypotension about 4.5-fold.

Pooled RCTs still can't prove IV lytics add benefit before thrombectomy (functional independence 51% vs 48%, not significant), but the symptomatic ICH increase wasn't significant either. Keep giving lytics to eligible patients while thrombectomy is arranged.

articles.takeaway: Fentanyl and opioid-stimulant co-exposure tripled the odds of an ED naloxone infusion after overdose
articles.title: Factors associated with continuous naloxone infusion use following opioid overdose in the emergency department.
articles.population: 1,165 ED encounters for nonfatal opioid overdose treated with naloxone, 1 US academic center (Alabama), 2019–2024
articles.summary: A naloxone infusion was started in 227 encounters (19.5%), and infusion use grew over the study period. After adjustment, a fentanyl-positive screen (aOR 2.96, 95% CI 1.92–4.57) and combined opioid-stimulant positivity (aOR 3.00) were linked to infusion use, while a positive opiate screen made it less likely (aOR 0.50). Prolonged infusions sometimes delivered large volumes of IV fluid. The design is observational, so the associations aren't causal.
articles.why: Fentanyl-era overdoses are pushing more infusions. A common starting rate is two-thirds of the bolus dose that reversed the patient, given per hour; ED pharmacists can concentrate the bag to limit fluid, titrate to breathing rather than full alertness, and reassess within a few hours instead of running it on autopilot.

articles.takeaway: Massive GHB exposures caused deep coma and frequent intubation, but nearly everyone survived with supportive care
articles.title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of massive gamma-hydroxybutyrate exposure in a multicentre emergency department cohort.
articles.population: 154 patients with whole-blood GHB of 300 mg/L or higher, 18 EDs in Victoria, Australia, Nov 2021–Mar 2026
articles.summary: Median GHB concentration was 380 mg/L, and 97% had other substances on board. Three-quarters had a first GCS of 3, 66% were intubated, 67% went to the ICU, a quarter were hypotensive and 20% needed vasopressors. Higher GHB levels predicted hypotension but not coma depth, and opioid co-detection was linked to hypotension (aOR 4.51) and hypoxemia (aOR 3.64). One patient died, and 27% were discharged directly from the ED.
articles.why: GHB coma is profound but usually short and reversible, so airway support and time are the treatment; there's no antidote, and flumazenil or physostigmine don't help. Watch for hypotension when opioids are also involved, and plan for withdrawal (which can need high-dose benzodiazepines or phenobarbital) in regular users.

articles.takeaway: Nearly a quarter of patients with kratom, phenibut or tianeptine exposure seen by toxicologists needed the ICU
articles.title: Clinical characteristics of unregulated psychoactive supplement exposures: a 15-year multicenter study of kratom, phenibut, and tianeptine.
articles.population: 152 encounters (97 kratom, 44 phenibut, 11 tianeptine) in the Toxicology Investigators Consortium registry, 2010–2024
articles.summary: Cases rose over time, and patients were mostly men (84%) with a median age of 35. Most use was intentional, for euphoria, self-treatment or managing withdrawal, and 48% had co-ingestants such as stimulants, opioids or other supplements. Overall, 23% were admitted to the ICU and one patient died. Only 10% got buprenorphine-naloxone and 10.5% got naloxone education or a prescription at discharge.
articles.why: These "gas station" products act on opioid or GABA receptors and don't show up on routine drug screens. Ask about them directly, treat kratom or tianeptine dependence like opioid use disorder (buprenorphine is an option), and send these patients home with naloxone.

articles.takeaway: IV lytics before thrombectomy nudged functional independence up 3 points, but the benefit wasn't statistically certain
articles.title: Intravenous thrombolysis prior to endovascular treatment for stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.population: 7 RCTs, 2,884 adults with large-vessel occlusion stroke eligible for IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours
articles.summary: Functional independence (mRS 0–2) was 51.2% with IV thrombolysis plus thrombectomy vs 48.0% with thrombectomy alone (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.99–1.15). A Bayesian analysis put the chance of any benefit at about 89%. Mortality was similar (RR 0.98), and symptomatic ICH was numerically higher with lytics but not significantly (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87–1.63). Neither superiority nor equivalence was shown.
articles.why: Supports current guidance to give tenecteplase or alteplase to eligible LVO patients without delaying transfer for thrombectomy. Stroke pharmacists should keep door-to-needle times fast and confirm the dose and time given before the patient leaves for the angio suite.

articles.takeaway: Sepsis steroid meta-analyses disagree mainly because they pool different trials; hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone consistently helped
articles.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study.
articles.population: 42 systematic reviews (2015–2025) covering 121 unique RCTs of corticosteroids in sepsis
articles.summary: More than half of pairs of reviews shared no trials at all, and only three pairs overlapped heavily. Of 38 reviews with a short-term mortality analysis, 39% found benefit and 61% didn't. The disagreement came entirely from reviews of broad, non-specific steroid strategies: reviews of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone consistently found benefit, and those of hydrocortisone, vitamin C and thiamine consistently found none. No single methods factor explained the split.
articles.why: When a guideline or attending cites a steroid meta-analysis, check which trials it pooled. For septic shock needing ongoing vasopressors, hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (with or without fludrocortisone 50 mcg daily) has the most consistent support.

articles.takeaway: Median opioid dose per ED discharge prescription rose from 60 to 75 MME during the pandemic years
articles.title: Opioid prescription patterns from 2019 to 2024: a multicenter analysis in Maryland, USA.
articles.population: 117,912 adults discharged with opioid prescriptions from 13 EDs and 1 urgent care, University of Maryland system, 2019–2024
articles.summary: The study compared weekly morphine-equivalent dose per patient before and during the pandemic. Median dose per patient rose from 60 to 75 (p<0.001). Excluding buprenorphine and methadone, prescribing jumped in 2020 and then leveled off; including them, it kept rising every year, likely reflecting growth in ED-initiated OUD treatment. There were no indication or outcome data.
articles.why: Separating MOUD from analgesic opioids matters when tracking ED prescribing: rising buprenorphine is a success, while rising analgesic doses aren't. Pharmacists can audit discharge opioid quantities against a 3-day default and push nonopioid-first regimens.

articles.takeaway: Requiring an indication on urine test orders cut ordering 30% and raised appropriate tests from 61% to 85%
articles.title: Impact of implementing an indication-based urinary tract infection diagnostic order menu at a veterans affairs facility.
articles.population: Adults with urinalysis or urine culture orders at 1 VA medical center (Palo Alto), Jun–Nov 2023 vs Jun–Nov 2024
articles.summary: A pharmacy-led stewardship team replaced free-text urine orders with a menu requiring a clinical indication. Urine test orders fell by about 30% per month, and appropriate ordering in an audited sample rose from 61% to 85% (p=0.0004). Treatment appropriateness, C. difficile, repeat testing and 30-day mortality didn't change significantly. Only 8% of post-period orders citing altered mental status met likely-UTI criteria.
articles.why: ED urine cultures in confused older adults drive a lot of asymptomatic bacteriuria treatment. An indication-required order is a low-effort stewardship fix ED pharmacists can champion, especially for altered mental status without urinary symptoms.

articles.takeaway: Selective digestive decontamination cut ICU-acquired infections by about a quarter, but neither it nor probiotics lowered mortality
articles.title: Gut microbiome-based interventions to prevent ICU-acquired infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: Adult ICU RCTs, 2000–2025: 9 selective digestive decontamination trials (19,907 patients) and 29 prebiotic/probiotic/synbiotic trials (5,483 patients)
articles.summary: Neither approach reduced mortality (SDD RR 0.96; biotics RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87–1.00). SDD reduced ICU-acquired infections (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60–0.98) and halved pneumonia (RR 0.50), while probiotics didn't significantly reduce infections overall (RR 0.82). Prebiotics or synbiotics lowered pneumonia (RR 0.70). The two strategies were compared only indirectly, and the probiotic trials varied widely.
articles.why: SDD remains a debated, resistance-sensitive strategy, and routine probiotics for ventilated patients still lack mortality benefit (and carry bacteremia risk in the immunocompromised). Expect stewardship pharmacists to weigh local resistance before adopting SDD for long ED boarders on ventilators.

issues.note: One sepsis RCT (CEMVIS, megadose vitamin C) leads a window that is otherwise mostly observational for ED pharmacotherapy. The other EM items are a Kcentra vs Balfaxar aPTT comparison, a Dutch multicenter ED intubation cohort, a meta-analysis on early VTE prophylaxis after traumatic brain bleeds and Australian wastewater data on illicit etomidate. Three RCTs outside the ED (apixaban in cirrhosis, DOAC prescribing alerts, rimegepant prevention) round out 8 picks.
bottom_line: Megadose IV vitamin C (12 g every 12 hours) didn't lower 28-day mortality in sepsis, caused more hypernatremia, and trended toward harm in septic shock. Keep it off ED and ICU sepsis order sets.

Starting pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis within 72 hours of a traumatic brain bleed was linked to about half the VTE with no rise in bleed progression, surgery or death across 18,500 patients (observational data).

Etomidate is showing up as an illicit adulterant and in vapes: Australian wastewater detections rose from 28% to 43% of samples as xylazine fell. Suspect it in overdoses with prolonged sedation, myoclonus or unexplained adrenal suppression.

articles.takeaway: Megadose IV vitamin C didn't reduce 28-day sepsis mortality and caused more hypernatremia
articles.title: Effect of megadose vitamin C in patients with sepsis: the CEMVIS randomized clinical trial.
articles.population: 231 adults with Sepsis-3 sepsis, 4 tertiary hospitals in China, 2022–2024
articles.summary: Patients were randomized, stratified by septic shock, to IV vitamin C 12 g every 12 hours for 4 days or placebo. 28-day mortality was 30.7% vs 31.0% (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.56–1.74), and ventilation, vasopressor and RRT duration and SOFA changes didn't differ. Hypernatremia was more common with vitamin C (35% vs 21%). A prespecified subgroup interaction suggested possible benefit without shock (15% vs 34% mortality) and possible harm with shock (39% vs 29%), with harm leaning stronger as lactate rose.
articles.why: Adds to LOVIT and VICTAS: high-dose vitamin C isn't a sepsis therapy, and it may hurt patients in shock. Pharmacists can remove it from sepsis protocols; vitamin C can also falsely raise point-of-care glucose readings.

articles.takeaway: Balfaxar's higher heparin content didn't raise aPTT more than Kcentra after DOAC or warfarin reversal
articles.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time following Kcentra® versus Balfaxar® reversal of apixaban, rivaroxaban, and warfarin: a propensity-score matched cohort study.
articles.population: 30 matched adults (15 per product) given 4F-PCC for apixaban, rivaroxaban or warfarin reversal with pre and post aPTT, 1 US center
articles.summary: Balfaxar contains roughly 2–10 times more heparin than Kcentra, so the authors checked whether it prolongs aPTT. Patients were matched on baseline aPTT and PCC dose. Median aPTT actually fell slightly with both (−1.2 s with Kcentra, −2.4 s with Balfaxar; difference not significant), and hemostatic effectiveness, 7-day clots and mortality didn't differ. The sample was very small and the confidence intervals were wide, so equivalence isn't proven.
articles.why: Reassuring for formularies that stock either 4F-PCC, and for pharmacists fielding questions about heparin content. Still avoid either product in patients with a history of HIT, since both contain heparin.

articles.takeaway: Dutch EDs hit 94% first-pass success with mostly video laryngoscopy and etomidate, but 1 in 7 had an adverse event
articles.title: Endotracheal intubation practices, success rates and adverse events in four Dutch emergency departments: a multicentre retrospective study.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med
articles.population: 1,250 ED intubations at 4 Dutch teaching hospitals, 2019–2023
articles.summary: Nearly half of intubations were after ROSC (47%), and video laryngoscopy (90%) and etomidate (74%) dominated. First-pass success was 93.8% regardless of operator specialty or training level. Adverse events occurred in 14.5%, mainly hypotension (6.5%) and desaturation (4.7%). Older age and a cardiac indication predicted hypotension, higher BMI and multiple attempts predicted desaturation, and lower pre-intubation SpO2 predicted peri-intubation arrest.
articles.why: Peri-intubation hypotension remains the most common complication even with etomidate. ED pharmacists can push for push-dose or infusion vasopressors drawn up before induction in older and post-arrest patients, plus reduced induction doses in shock.

articles.takeaway: Starting VTE prophylaxis within 72 hours of a traumatic brain bleed halved VTE without more bleed progression
articles.title: Early pharmacological thromboprophylaxis for patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 13 cohort studies, 18,554 patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage
articles.summary: Early prophylaxis was defined as starting within 72 hours of admission. It was associated with lower VTE (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.39–0.67) and no significant difference in ICH progression (OR 0.91), cranial surgery (OR 1.15) or in-hospital mortality (OR 0.99). All included studies were observational, so residual confounding (healthier patients getting earlier prophylaxis) is likely.
articles.why: Supports a protocolized start of enoxaparin (commonly 30–40 mg SC, often 24–72 hours after a stable repeat CT) rather than open-ended delays in TBI patients admitted from the ED. Pharmacists can prompt the team to set the start time at admission.

articles.takeaway: Etomidate appeared in Australian wastewater and spread as xylazine detections fell from 41% to 5%
articles.title: Emerging Trends in Etomidate and Xylazine: Wastewater-Based Monitoring Reveals the First Detection of Etomidate in Australia.
articles.population: 936 influent wastewater samples from metropolitan and regional Australian catchments, Apr 2025–Apr 2026
articles.summary: Xylazine was found in 188 samples and etomidate in 183. Xylazine detection fell steadily from 41% to 5% over the year, while etomidate detection in major cities rose from 28% to 43% and spread to regional areas. Wastewater detection came before other surveillance systems picked up etomidate. The data show population-level presence, not individual exposures or harms.
articles.why: Illicit etomidate (in fentanyl and in vapes, already reported in Asia) can cause prolonged sedation, myoclonus and adrenal suppression that naloxone won't fix. Consider a cortisol check and stress-dose hydrocortisone in refractory hypotension after unexplained sedative exposures; routine drug screens won't detect it.

articles.takeaway: Low-dose apixaban cut hepatic decompensation by about 21 points in Child-Pugh B/C cirrhosis without more bleeding
articles.title: Apixaban reduces hepatic decompensation in patients with cirrhosis (ApiHep): A randomized controlled trial.
articles.population: 134 adults aged 18–60 with Child-Pugh B7–C10 cirrhosis and no portal vein thrombosis, India
articles.summary: Patients got apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus standard therapy or standard therapy alone for 12 months. Hepatic decompensation at 1 year was 33.1% vs 54.3% (absolute risk reduction 21.2%, 95% CI 4.5–38.2). Ascites, encephalopathy and variceal bleeding were numerically lower but not individually significant, and mortality didn't differ. Any bleeding (42% vs 46%) and major bleeding (9% vs 12%) were similar.
articles.why: Cirrhosis patients on apixaban will increasingly show up in the ED with GI bleeds. Know the reversal plan (4F-PCC or andexanet) and that apixaban is generally avoided in Child-Pugh C outside trials like this one.

articles.takeaway: Interruptive DOAC dosing alerts cut inappropriate prescribing system-wide; adding a pharmacist referral link didn't help
articles.title: Use of Synchronous, Interruptive Electronic Health Record-Embedded Medication Alerts to Improve Evidence-Based Medication Prescribing: Randomized Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Two Prescriber Alerts.
articles.population: 286 prescribers (758 alerts) writing inappropriate ambulatory apixaban or rivaroxaban orders, 1 large US academic health system
articles.summary: Prescribers were randomized to an interruptive alert with or without an embedded clinical pharmacist referral option. About 29% of alerts led to a prescription change within 7 days, with no difference between arms (difference 1 point, 95% CI −7 to 9). System-wide, inappropriate DOAC prescriptions dropped by 3.5 percentage points (to 9.7%) right after alert launch. 30-day adverse events were uncommon and similar.
articles.why: Well-designed point-of-order alerts can catch routine DOAC dose errors (wrong renal or age dose), freeing pharmacists for complex cases. Wrong-dose DOACs are common at ED discharge, so these rules are worth building into ED order entry.

articles.takeaway: Daily rimegepant cut about 1.8 more monthly migraine days than placebo; every-other-day dosing helped less
articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of 2 Rimegepant Dosing Regimens for the Prevention of Episodic Migraine: A Randomized Controlled Study.
articles.population: 692 adults with episodic migraine (4–14 attacks a month), sites in 10 countries
articles.summary: Participants got placebo, rimegepant 75 mg every other day, or rimegepant 75 mg daily for 12 weeks. Both regimens beat placebo on monthly migraine days (−0.6 days every other day; −1.8 days daily). All five key secondary endpoints were met with daily dosing, but not with every-other-day dosing. Most adverse events were mild or moderate.
articles.why: More ED migraine patients will be on a daily gepant. Rimegepant is a CYP3A4 substrate, so watch strong inhibitors like clarithromycin or azoles, and gepants can be used alongside ED migraine cocktails (dopamine antagonists, NSAIDs).

issues.note: No ED drug RCTs this window, so this issue runs 8 picks led by two meta-analyses (prehospital TXA and adjunct intra-arterial thrombolysis after thrombectomy). The other EM items are a droperidol agitation review, a pediatric methemoglobinemia series, a PE catheter-lytic bleeding score and the clinical fallout of the 2024–25 IV fluid shortage; a driving-risk medication study and an ICU GI bleeding analysis round it out.
bottom_line: Pooling the three prehospital RCTs, early TXA in trauma was linked to about 19% lower 30-day mortality, with no significant rise in clots or seizures. The TBI-specific estimate rests on one trial and remains uncertain.

Droperidol is back as a first-line option for severe ED agitation: in pooled data it sedated about twice as many patients by 15 minutes as ziprasidone or lorazepam, with less respiratory depression and clinically significant QT prolongation in only about 1%.

In infants with methemoglobinemia, topical lidocaine and prilocaine (often around circumcision) caused most cases. Methylene blue lowered levels further than IV ascorbic acid, and an unexplained case should prompt a look for congenital CYB5R3 deficiency.

articles.takeaway: Prehospital TXA was linked to about 19% lower 30-day mortality across three trauma RCTs, without a clear clot signal
articles.title: Prehospital tranexamic acid in trauma and traumatic brain injury: a systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized comparative evidence.
articles.population: 21 reports reviewed; RCT-only pooled analysis of PATCH-Trauma, STAAMP and ROC-TXA
articles.summary: The authors pooled only independent randomized trials for efficacy and summarized observational data separately. Prehospital TXA was associated with lower 28- or 30-day mortality (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68–0.95). The TBI estimate came from ROC-TXA alone and wasn't significant (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.64–1.20). Thromboembolic events and seizures weren't significantly increased, but DVT and PE point estimates leaned toward harm with wide intervals.
articles.why: Supports giving TXA early (1 g IV over 10 minutes, ideally within 1 hour and no later than 3 hours from injury) in bleeding trauma, including in the field. ED pharmacists should confirm the time of any prehospital dose so the second gram (1 g over 8 hours) isn't missed or doubled.

articles.takeaway: Droperidol sedated agitated ED patients faster than ziprasidone or lorazepam, with rare QT problems
articles.title: The Role of Droperidol in the Management of Acute Agitation: A Comprehensive Review.
articles.population: RCTs, systematic reviews and observational studies of droperidol for acute agitation, 2000–2025
articles.summary: Droperidol worked within 3–10 minutes, and 64% of patients were adequately sedated at 15 minutes vs 25–35% with ziprasidone and 29% with lorazepam. Respiratory depression was less common (12% vs 36–39% with ziprasidone and 48% with lorazepam). QT prolongation occurred in 1.3% of 1,009 patients, mostly those with existing risk factors, and torsades was very rare in large series. Adding midazolam sped sedation and cut rescue medication use (41% vs 62%).
articles.why: Supports droperidol (commonly 5–10 mg IM/IV in adults, lower in older patients) as a first-line agent for severe agitation, per ACEP. Get an ECG once the patient is calm, check for other QT-prolonging drugs and low potassium or magnesium, and consider pairing it with midazolam.

articles.takeaway: Infant methemoglobinemia was mostly caused by local anesthetics; methylene blue lowered levels more than IV vitamin C
articles.title: Pediatric methemoglobinemia in the emergency department: etiology, treatment patterns, and short-term outcomes.
articles.population: 24 children with methemoglobin of 5% or more (median age 4 months, 88% male), 1 Turkish pediatric ED, 2022–2025
articles.summary: Median SpO2 was 88% and median initial methemoglobin 25.5%. Drug exposure explained 79% of cases, mostly lidocaine (10) and prilocaine (7), often around circumcision, and 4 of the 5 patients without an exposure had pathogenic or likely pathogenic CYB5R3 variants. Post-treatment methemoglobin was lower with methylene blue (11 patients) than IV ascorbic acid (13 patients), 2.6% vs 7.8%, though relative reduction didn't differ significantly. The treatment comparison was small and exploratory.
articles.why: Think methemoglobinemia in a cyanotic infant with SpO2 stuck near 85–88% after a procedure or topical anesthetic. Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes is first-line; screen for G6PD deficiency when possible and use ascorbic acid if methylene blue is contraindicated. Watch benzocaine and lidocaine sprays before pediatric intubation.

articles.takeaway: Adding intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy raised excellent 90-day outcomes from 37% to 45%
articles.title: Adjunct Intra-Arterial Thrombolysis following Endovascular Thrombectomy in Different Patient Subgroups: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Ten Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.population: 10 RCTs, 2,988 patients with acute ischemic stroke treated with thrombectomy with or without adjunct IA lytic
articles.summary: Excellent functional outcome (mRS 0–1 at 90 days) occurred in 44.9% with adjunct IA thrombolysis vs 36.9% with thrombectomy alone (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.10–1.35). Functional independence, symptomatic ICH and mortality didn't differ significantly, but the intervals couldn't rule out meaningful harm. The effect didn't vary by bridging IV lytic, alteplase vs tenecteplase or reperfusion grade, and it was significant only for anterior circulation occlusions.
articles.why: Pooled data now favor adjunct IA lytics after anterior-circulation thrombectomy, but the basilar trial INSIST-IT (Nov 8 issue) stopped early for safety. Stroke pharmacists preparing IA alteplase or tenecteplase should confirm the occlusion site and total lytic dose given.

articles.takeaway: A four-item score (female, hypertension, age, high-risk PE) flagged patients with triple the bleeding risk after catheter-directed lytics
articles.title: Major Bleeding After Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis for Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Derivation and Transferability of the F-HARP Risk Assessment Model.
articles.population: 1,246 patients from 16 cohorts and trials of catheter-directed thrombolysis for PE; external cohort of 566 from RIETE
articles.summary: Major bleeding occurred in 6.0% of the derivation cohort, including 10 intracranial hemorrhages. The F-HARP model (female sex, hypertension, age, high-risk PE) had an optimism-corrected AUROC of 0.70. In the independent cohort, high-risk patients bled more often within 30 days (11.2% vs 3.8%; OR 3.18), but discrimination was modest (AUROC 0.64) and calibration imperfect.
articles.why: Useful context during PERT discussions about catheter-directed lytics for intermediate- or high-risk PE. Pharmacists can flag high F-HARP patients for tighter heparin anti-Xa monitoring, lower lytic doses and close neuro checks; the authors say it isn't ready for precise risk estimates.

articles.takeaway: During the post-Hurricane Helene IV fluid shortage, ED patients had slightly more sepsis, AKI and admissions
articles.title: Clinical Outcomes Associated With Intravenous Fluid Shortages in Emergency Department Patients: A Propensity Score Matched Cohort Study.
articles.population: About 2.77 million matched adult ED patients per group, aged 18–65, shortage (Oct 2024–May 2025) vs prior adequate-supply period
articles.summary: Fluid administration fell during the shortage (HR 0.87), as expected. Within 7 days, shortage-period visits were linked to small increases in sepsis (HR 1.07), gastroenteritis (HR 1.15), hyponatremia (HR 1.07), AKI (HR 1.01) and hospitalization (HR 1.06), with no difference in mortality. The authors note the effects are statistically significant but small for individual patients, and period-to-period differences may be confounded.
articles.why: Conservation strategies like oral rehydration for mild dehydration, IV push instead of piggyback for compatible drugs and smaller diluent volumes appeared mostly safe at the population level. The sepsis and admission signals argue for protecting fluid supply for resuscitation first in the next shortage.

articles.takeaway: A third of injured road users in the ED had taken a prescription drug that day; muscle relaxants carried the highest crash risk
articles.title: Prescription drugs and the risk of road traffic crashes in Bordeaux, France: a study matching emergency department health reports and a pharmaceutical reimbursement registry.
articles.population: 17,296 drivers and vulnerable road users seen within 24 hours of a crash, 1 French university hospital ED, 2013–2021
articles.summary: On the day of the crash, 32.9% had been exposed to at least one prescription drug. Drugs in France's highest driving-risk tier (level 3) were linked to crashes in the case-crossover analysis, especially anxiolytics, opioids and antidepressants. In the case-control analysis, level 2 (aOR 1.27) and level 3 (aOR 1.43) drugs raised risk, and centrally acting muscle relaxants carried the highest odds (aOR 2.26). About 4% of crashes were attributable to these medications.
articles.why: ED discharge prescriptions for opioids, benzodiazepines and muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine need explicit no-driving counseling, especially for the first doses and when combined. It is another reason to leave muscle relaxants off routine back pain discharges.

articles.takeaway: Clinically important upper GI bleeding in ventilated ICU patients was linked to about 56% higher ICU mortality
articles.title: ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis.
articles.population: 4,821 invasively ventilated adults in an international pantoprazole vs placebo stress ulcer prophylaxis trial
articles.summary: Clinically important upper GI bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%). Median ICU stay was 19 days with bleeding vs 9 days without. Treating bleeding as a time-dependent event to avoid immortal time bias, it was associated with higher ICU mortality (HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.13–2.15) after adjusting for severity, organ support and randomized pantoprazole assignment.
articles.why: Shows these bleeds aren't benign, which supports stress ulcer prophylaxis (e.g., pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily) in ventilated patients, including ED boarders. Reassess the indication at extubation and transfer so prophylaxis doesn't continue unneeded.

issues.note: A thin Tuesday window with one small ED RCT (a nerve block vs IV fentanyl pilot) and otherwise observational or review evidence, so this issue runs 8 picks. The EM items cover analgesia, sepsis antibiotic timing, ICH blood pressure, ED OUD bridge programs and kratom; a GLP-1 aspiration pharmacovigilance study and a Cochrane G-CSF review round it out.
bottom_line: For scapular fractures, an ultrasound-guided suprascapular block beat IV fentanyl 1 mcg/kg by about 4 pain points at 30–60 minutes and cut rescue analgesia from 79% to 13% in a small pilot RCT. Regional blocks belong in the ED analgesia toolkit for shoulder-girdle injuries.

In 62,000 ED sepsis encounters, only about 3% got antibiotics within 1 hour, and a clear mortality penalty appeared only past 24 hours. That doesn't loosen the 1-hour goal for septic shock, but it shows how far real-world timing sits from the guideline.
A six-element standard now defines a true ED bridge program: same-day buprenorphine, a bedside take-home supply, 24/7 coverage, dedicated staff space, a warm handoff and naloxone at every visit.

articles.takeaway: Suprascapular nerve block gave much better pain relief than IV fentanyl for scapular fractures, with far less rescue analgesia
articles.title: Ultrasound-Guided Suprascapular Nerve Block Versus Intravenous Fentanyl for Analgesia in Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Traumatic Scapular Fractures.
articles.population: 60 adults with traumatic scapular fractures and pain scores of 7 or higher, 1 Level I trauma center ED in North India
articles.summary: Patients were randomized to an ultrasound-guided suprascapular nerve block or IV fentanyl 1 mcg/kg. Median pain at 30 minutes was 3 with the block vs 7 with fentanyl, a 4-point difference that held at 60 minutes and narrowed to 1 point by 6 hours. Rescue analgesia was needed in 13% vs 79%, and drowsiness was more common with fentanyl (12 vs 2 patients). It is a small single-center open-label pilot.
articles.why: Supports regional blocks as an opioid-sparing first option for shoulder-girdle fractures. ED pharmacists can support block programs with local anesthetic dosing limits (e.g., ropivacaine or bupivacaine max mg/kg), LAST recognition and lipid emulsion 20% kept at the bedside.

articles.takeaway: Only 2.8% of ED sepsis patients got antibiotics within 1 hour; mortality rose clearly only when the first dose came after 24 hours
articles.title: Time to Antibiotic Administration in the Treatment of Sepsis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.population: 62,153 adult ED encounters with severe sepsis or septic shock, US hospital system, Dec 2023–Dec 2025
articles.summary: Time to first antibiotic was grouped into under 1, 1–3, 4–12, 13–24 and over 24 hours. Compared with under 1 hour, in-hospital mortality didn't differ significantly for any window up to 24 hours, but was higher after 24 hours (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.18–1.95). Length of stay among survivors grew with delay, about 9% longer at 13–24 hours and 56% longer past 24 hours. Severe sepsis and shock were analyzed together, and sicker patients likely got faster treatment, which can mask harm from moderate delays.
articles.why: This shouldn't be read as permission to wait in septic shock, where the 2026 SSC goal is still within 1 hour. It does show how rarely that goal is met; ED pharmacists can close the gap with antibiotics stocked in automated cabinets, first-dose IV push beta-lactams and order sets that don't hold the dose for cultures.

articles.takeaway: Continuous labetalol infusion reached SBP under 140 in a median of 2 hours in ICH; bradycardia was the main adverse effect
articles.title: Assessment of safety and effectiveness of continuous intravenous labetalol infusion for blood pressure control in patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: a STROBE-compliant observational study.
articles.population: 84 adults with spontaneous ICH on continuous labetalol targeting BP under 140/90, 1 Thai center
articles.summary: Median time to target BP was 2 hours, and patients spent a median of 53% of the first 24 hours at target. Hematoma expansion occurred in 8.3%. Nineteen patients had 42 adverse events, most often bradycardia (22.6%), but none needed resuscitation, and rates were similar above and below 300 mg cumulative dose in 24 hours. Lower baseline SBP and heart rate and diabetes predicted adverse events. There was no comparison group.
articles.why: A practical option when nicardipine or clevidipine is short or unavailable. Check baseline heart rate before starting, hold or reduce for HR under about 60, and expect to need more frequent titration since time at target was only about half.

articles.takeaway: Most EDs treated sickle cell pain about as fast as renal colic, but 28% delayed it by a median of 19 minutes
articles.title: Assessing Differences in Timeliness of Emergency Department Pain Treatment for Adult Sickle Cell Pain and Renal Colic.
articles.population: 436,692 sickle cell VOE and 5.6 million renal colic encounters at 103 US adult EDs, 2019–2025
articles.summary: The study applied ASH's new site-level quality measure: median time to first pain medication for sickle cell VOE minus that for renal colic. The median gap was +4 minutes, with 56% of sites equivalent (within 10 minutes), 16% faster for sickle cell and 28% slower (median gap +19 minutes, worst +91). The gap wasn't related to sickle cell volume, ED length of stay or admission rates. It sets the first national baseline for this measure.
articles.why: A ready-made benchmark for ED pharmacists to track locally. Pairs with yesterday's EHR-flag study: structured protocols such as individualized care plans, nurse-initiated IN fentanyl and pre-verified opioid orders are what move this number.

articles.takeaway: Review defines six essential elements of an ED bridge program, starting with same-day buprenorphine and a take-home supply
articles.title: What makes a bridge program a bridge program? Toward evidence-based standards for emergency department-initiated opioid use disorder treatment.
articles.population: Narrative synthesis of studies, consensus statements and implementation reports through May 2026
articles.summary: The authors argue that 'bridge program' has become a catch-all label and propose six required elements: same-day medication initiation, bedside dispensing of a short medication supply before discharge, 24/7 coverage, dedicated on-site workspace for program staff, a warm handoff to outpatient care, and naloxone at every ED encounter. Programs missing these elements may still help but aren't delivering the evidence-based model, and their outcomes may reflect that. It's a framework, not new outcome data.
articles.why: Bedside dispensing and naloxone at every encounter are pharmacy-owned pieces. ED pharmacists can build take-home buprenorphine packs, standing naloxone dispensing and an induction order set that covers high-dose starts for fentanyl-era patients.

articles.takeaway: Maternal kratom use caused neonatal opioid withdrawal, and most affected newborns needed morphine or methadone
articles.title: A National Poison Data System description of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome related to maternal kratom use.
articles.population: 14 neonates under 21 days old with in utero kratom exposure reported to US poison centers, 2015–2023
articles.summary: Of 20 reported neonatal kratom exposures, 14 met inclusion. Symptoms included agitation, tremor, increased tone, tachypnea, poor feeding and weight loss, with a median duration of 8 days. Nine of 14 received opioid treatment, usually morphine and/or methadone, typically starting 1–3 days after the poison center consult. The data predate the spread of concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products, so current risk may be higher.
articles.why: Kratom isn't caught on standard urine drug screens, so ask about it directly in pregnant ED patients and in newborns with unexplained withdrawal signs. It's another reason to include kratom in med histories alongside opioid and buprenorphine questions.

articles.takeaway: GLP-1 RA users had a numerically higher but nonsignificant aspiration signal in perioperative FAERS reports; opioids doubled the odds
articles.title: Perioperative pulmonary aspiration reports associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists: a pharmacovigilance analysis of FAERS.
articles.population: 41,308 deduplicated perioperative FAERS reports (158 GLP-1 RA, 174 SGLT2i), 2016–March 2024
articles.summary: Reports listing a general anesthetic or neuromuscular blocker were used as a stand-in for the perioperative setting. Aspiration reporting odds were not significantly higher with GLP-1 RAs (ROR 1.27; adjusted OR 2.08, P = 0.19), with very few events. Concomitant opioid use was independently linked to aspiration (aOR 2.12, P < 0.001). Spontaneous reports can't give incidence, and the authors call the results hypothesis-generating.
articles.why: Absence of a significant signal isn't proof of safety, given how few events there were. For ED sedation and RSI in GLP-1 RA users, still ask about the last dose and GI symptoms, consider gastric ultrasound or RSI precautions, and minimize stacked opioids.

articles.takeaway: Primary G-CSF prophylaxis cut infections by about a third in solid tumors but didn't improve survival and tripled bone pain
articles.title: Prophylactic granulopoiesis-stimulating factors for people with solid tumors undergoing cancer treatment.
articles.population: 26 RCTs, 5,320 adults with solid tumors on identical chemotherapy with vs without primary G-CSF or GM-CSF
articles.summary: Primary prophylaxis likely reduced infection risk (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49–0.83; moderate certainty). It made little or no difference to overall survival (HR 0.85, low certainty) or to all-cause mortality during chemotherapy (RR 0.92, moderate certainty). Bone pain was likely much more common (RR 3.55). No trial reported quality of life.
articles.why: Explains a common ED complaint: severe bone pain a few days after pegfilgrastim, which often responds to an NSAID or loratadine. In febrile neutropenia, prior G-CSF doesn't change the need for antipseudomonal antibiotics within 1 hour.

issues.note: A thin Monday window for ED pharmacotherapy, with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs 8 picks with several reviews. The EM items are a sickle cell analgesia-timing study, a trauma anticoagulation review, a poison center mushroom series and an ICU sepsis antibiotic dosing review. Two large pediatric obesity RCTs (NEJM, JAMA), a stewardship de-escalation cohort and a QT interaction study fill out the rest.
bottom_line: A colored EHR flag for sickle cell patients didn't speed first opioid doses for vaso-occlusive crisis (about 66–72 minutes either way). Getting under the 60-minute goal likely takes nurse-initiated or pharmacist-built standing protocols, not a passive alert.
Rapid-onset sweating, drooling and GI symptoms after foraged mushrooms point to muscarine; atropine reverses the dangerous bradycardia and hypotension, and severe cases can die before reaching care.

In a high-resistance hospital, de-escalation was withheld in nearly half of patients whose cultures allowed it, while patients who were de-escalated had fewer adverse events and less AKI. That gap is a ready-made target for stewardship pharmacists.

articles.takeaway: A passive EHR color flag didn't shorten time to first opioid for sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis
articles.title: Impact of an electronic health record visual cue on time to analgesia in patients with sickle cell in vaso-occlusive crisis.
articles.population: 841 ED encounters from 168 adults with sickle cell VOC, 1 large US urban academic ED, 1 year
articles.summary: The ED added a salmon-colored EHR marker to identify patients with sickle cell disease and prompt faster treatment of pain crises. Mean time from arrival to first opioid was 66.3 minutes before and 71.7 minutes after (adjusted difference +2.5 minutes, 95% CI −4.2 to 9.2). The odds of getting an opioid within 60 minutes didn't change (aOR 0.97), and results held after excluding frequent visitors at several thresholds. It is a single-center retrospective before-and-after study.
articles.why: ASH guidelines call for analgesia within 60 minutes of arrival. ED pharmacists can help close the gap with individualized pain plans in the chart, nurse-initiated IN fentanyl or SC/IV hydromorphone protocols, and pre-verified order sets rather than relying on visual cues.

articles.takeaway: Review lays out a stepwise ED approach to injured patients on anticoagulants, with agent-specific reversal
articles.title: Management of the Anticoagulated Trauma Patient.
articles.population: Review of ED evaluation and reversal for trauma patients on preinjury anticoagulation (4–7% of trauma patients)
articles.summary: Preinjury anticoagulant use, now mostly DOACs, is present in about 4–7% of trauma patients and raises the risk of bleeding complications and death. The authors walk through the primary and secondary surveys, stressing fast identification of the agent and a low threshold for CT. They cover agent-specific labs, transfusion principles and tailored reversal for warfarin, factor Xa inhibitors and dabigatran.
articles.why: Pharmacists drive this workflow: confirm the agent, dose and last dose time, then match reversal (4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K for warfarin, andexanet or 4F-PCC for factor Xa inhibitors, idarucizumab for dabigatran). Keep a weight-based PCC dosing reference at the trauma bay.

articles.takeaway: Muscarinic mushroom poisoning was rare but caused rapid cholinergic toxicity, one atropine-responsive shock and one death
articles.title: A 25-Year Analysis of Muscarinic Mushroom Poisoning in Wisconsin.
articles.population: 9 confirmed cases among mushroom exposures reported to the Wisconsin Poison Center, 2000–2025
articles.summary: Two reviewers applied a strict clinical case definition, and 5 of the 9 cases had expert mushroom identification (Clitocybe in 3, Inocybe in 2). Symptoms started quickly, led by sweating and excess salivation, then GI upset. Two patients had severe cardiovascular effects: one with bradycardia and hypotension that responded to atropine, and one who died after cardiovascular collapse before treatment. All 8 survivors recovered fully.
articles.why: Early-onset cholinergic symptoms after foraged mushrooms suggest muscarine rather than amatoxin, which typically has a delay of 6 hours or more. Titrate IV atropine (adults often start at 1 mg, repeated as needed) to dry secretions and restore heart rate, and call poison control for identification help.

articles.takeaway: Loading doses, prolonged infusions and drug-level monitoring should be standard for antibiotics in ICU sepsis
articles.title: Refining antibiotic dosing regimens for the treatment of sepsis in critically ill patients in the intensive care unit.
articles.population: Literature review (Ovid Medline, April 2026) of antibiotic dose optimization in critically ill adults with sepsis
articles.summary: Critical illness changes volume of distribution and clearance in ways that often leave antibiotic exposure too low or too high. The authors review loading doses, prolonged beta-lactam infusions, dosing nomograms, therapeutic drug monitoring and model-informed precision dosing. They recommend these tools as a foundation of sepsis care, especially in patients with large PK changes, suspected toxicity or treatment failure, or high-MIC pathogens, while noting that exposure targets and outcome links still need work.
articles.why: The ED sets the first exposure. Give full loading doses regardless of renal function (e.g., vancomycin 20–35 mg/kg, full first beta-lactam dose), and hand off to extended infusions and AUC- or level-guided dosing once the patient is admitted.

articles.takeaway: Only 28% of inpatients on empiric IV antibiotics were de-escalated, and it was withheld in 46% of eligible cases
articles.title: Real-life de-escalation practices in the era of high antimicrobial resistance rates: Insights from a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.population: 468 hospitalized adults on empiric IV antibiotics for suspected infection, 1 Turkish tertiary center, Jan–Jul 2024
articles.summary: Courses were grouped by change in Antibiotic Spectrum Index into de-escalation, no change or escalation. De-escalated patients had the best clinical response (99% vs 93% vs 85%) and the fewest adverse events (6% vs 12% vs 30%) and AKI (5% vs 10% vs 25%), and 90-day mortality was higher in the no-change (HR 4.1) and escalation (HR 6.7) groups. New resistance at 90 days didn't differ. Because sicker patients are less likely to be de-escalated, the authors present these as practice-gap data rather than a treatment effect.
articles.why: Clinical instability, poor source control and a second infection site were the main reasons de-escalation was skipped. Pharmacist culture follow-up at 48–72 hours, including for patients admitted from the ED, is the obvious fix.

articles.takeaway: Weekly semaglutide cut BMI by about 16 points more than placebo in children aged 6 to 11
articles.title: Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity in Children 6 to <12 Years of Age.
articles.population: 167 children aged 6 to under 12 with obesity, randomized 2:1 to semaglutide or placebo for 104 weeks (STEP Young)
articles.summary: At week 68, BMI changed by −13.5% with semaglutide vs +2.7% with placebo (difference −16.2 points, 95% CI −19.4 to −12.9). BMI dropped below the obesity threshold in 38% vs 2%, and the effect held at week 104 (difference −17.8 points). Adverse events were common in both arms (96% vs 93%), GI effects were more frequent with semaglutide, and only 1 child stopped because of them. The trial was funded by Novo Nordisk.
articles.why: GLP-1 RA use is about to extend into elementary-age children. In the ED, ask about it in kids with vomiting, dehydration or abdominal pain, and remember delayed gastric emptying when planning procedural sedation.

articles.takeaway: Tirzepatide lowered BMI by about 19% vs placebo in adolescents with obesity over 72 weeks
articles.title: Tirzepatide in Adolescents With Obesity: The SURMOUNT-ADOLESCENTS Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.population: 160 adolescents aged 12–17 with obesity, or overweight with a complication, 31 sites in 6 countries
articles.summary: Participants were randomized 2:1 to weekly tirzepatide titrated to 5, 10 or 15 mg, or placebo, plus lifestyle support. At week 72, BMI fell 18.5% with tirzepatide vs a 0.5% rise with placebo (difference −19.0 points, 95% CI −23.9 to −14.1). About 80% of tirzepatide patients lost at least 5% of BMI vs 29% on placebo, and all 10 key secondary outcomes favored tirzepatide. GI adverse events were the most common and mostly mild to moderate.
articles.why: Puts a second incretin agent on track for adolescent use. ED pharmacists should add GLP-1/GIP agents to med history questions for teens and counsel on GI effects, dehydration risk and aspiration precautions before sedation.

articles.takeaway: About 1 in 6 patients on oral anticancer drugs had a potential QT-prolonging drug interaction
articles.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Potential QT-Interval-Prolonging Drug-Drug Interactions in Patients Receiving Oral Anticancer Drugs.
articles.population: 1,732 patients with advanced cancer on at least 1 oral anticancer drug, EHR data from 1 US cancer program
articles.summary: Overall, 17.1% had at least one potential QT interaction during oral anticancer therapy. Of those, 47.5% were pharmacodynamic only (two QT-prolonging drugs), 21.2% pharmacokinetic only (CYP or transporter effects) and 31.3% both. About half involved the anticancer drug itself, most often pazopanib, palbociclib and vandetanib. The study counted overlapping prescriptions, not actual QT changes or arrhythmias.
articles.why: Oncology patients come to the ED with nausea, infection and agitation, where ondansetron, haloperidol, droperidol, azoles and fluoroquinolones pile on QT risk. Check the oral chemo list and a baseline ECG before stacking these drugs.

issues.note: A very thin Sunday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 7 picks rather than padding. The EM items are an ED buprenorphine follow-up cohort, updated Scandinavian head injury guidelines that relax CT rules for DOAC patients, a pediatric intra-arrest blood pressure meta-analysis and a whiplash medication-trajectory cohort. Three stewardship and anticoagulation papers round it out; all are observational or reviews.
bottom_line: After ED-initiated buprenorphine, every extra day of waiting for the first clinic visit raised the odds of a no-show by about 31%, and attendance fell below 50% once the wait passed 3 days. Book follow-up within 72 hours and bridge the prescription to that date.

New Scandinavian head injury guidelines no longer push routine CT for every mild head injury on a DOAC, and add GFAP/UCH-L1 biomarkers and structured observation as options. Warfarin and antiplatelet patients still need a careful risk check.
Stable patients with uncomplicated Enterobacterales bacteremia did as well switching to oral antibiotics by day 4 as later, with 2 fewer hospital days and 3 fewer antibiotic days.

articles.takeaway: Each extra day between ED buprenorphine and the first clinic visit cut follow-up attendance; 3 days was the tipping point
articles.title: Longer wait times after ED-initiated buprenorphine associated with lower appointment attendance.
articles.population: 301 adults given observed ED buprenorphine induction or a buprenorphine prescription, 1 US ED, 2019–2025
articles.summary: Only about half of patients (51%) made it to their first outpatient MOUD appointment. Demographics, insurance, primary opioid, polysubstance use and whether induction was observed or unobserved weren't linked to attendance. Each added day of waiting raised the adjusted odds of missing the visit by 31% (aOR 1.31, 95% CI 1.10–1.56), and the probability of attending dropped to 50% at a 3-day wait. It is a single-center retrospective study.
articles.why: The biggest lever after ED induction may be scheduling, not dosing. ED pharmacists can push for next-day or 72-hour bridge clinic slots, write the bridge prescription to cover the full gap, and add naloxone to every discharge.

articles.takeaway: Updated Scandinavian head injury guidelines drop routine CT for many DOAC patients and add blood biomarkers
articles.title: The Scandinavian Neurotrauma Committee 2026 guidelines for initial management of minimal, mild and moderate head injuries in adults: a systematic review, meta-analysis and modified Delphi consensus study.
articles.population: Adults with minimal, mild or moderate head injury in the ED; GRADE-rated review plus 29-stakeholder Delphi panel
articles.summary: The committee's first update since 2013 was driven largely by an aging population and wider antithrombotic use. A GRADE-based systematic review and meta-analysis fed a modified Delphi process that produced seven recommendations and new flowcharts for CT, discharge, observation and repeat imaging. Key changes are less emphasis on routine CT for patients on DOACs, use of GFAP and UCH-L1 biomarkers to rule out intracranial injury, and structured observation instead of CT for some risk groups. The authors note the new pathways still need validation.
articles.why: Med history drives the head injury pathway, so pharmacists should confirm the exact anticoagulant or antiplatelet, dose and last dose time at triage. The relaxed DOAC stance doesn't extend to warfarin, and reversal agents (4F-PCC, andexanet, idarucizumab) should still be ready if a bleed is found.

articles.takeaway: A diastolic BP of at least 25 (infants) or 30 mm Hg (children) during pediatric CPR tracked with better survival
articles.title: Intra-arrest blood pressure monitoring during paediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.population: 6 observational studies of children with in-hospital cardiac arrest and arterial lines; 2 studies (577 events) pooled
articles.summary: Averaged over the first 10 minutes of CPR, a diastolic pressure of 25 mm Hg or more in infants and 30 mm Hg or more in older children was associated with higher ROSC, survival to discharge and survival with good neurologic outcome. Systolic thresholds showed no significant association. Certainty was very low, and the authors stress the data don't prove that titrating CPR or drugs to these targets improves outcomes.
articles.why: When a child arrests with an arterial line in place, diastolic pressure is a real-time readout of CPR and epinephrine effect. It can guide compression quality and epinephrine timing (0.01 mg/kg every 3–5 minutes), but it shouldn't replace standard dosing intervals.

articles.takeaway: After whiplash, a quarter of new opioid users and 43% of new sedative users went on to persistent use
articles.title: Trajectories of medication use after whiplash injury: high rates of persistent opioid and sedative use.
articles.population: 167 adults with motor vehicle collision whiplash injury, 1 Danish center, linked to national prescription data 12 months before and after
articles.summary: The share of patients filling nonopioid analgesics rose from 19% to 35% and opioids from 34% to 51% after the crash, while sedative-hypnotic use rose only slightly (13% to 17%). Among new users, 26% of opioid users and 43% of sedative-hypnotic users became persistent users. Higher early pain and disability scores predicted more medication use, and women were more likely to start and stay on opioids. The cohort was small and from one center.
articles.why: Whiplash is a common ED discharge diagnosis where short courses quietly become long ones. Favor NSAIDs, acetaminophen and early activity, keep any opioid or sedative supply to a few days, and flag high pain or disability scores for early follow-up.

articles.takeaway: Switching to oral antibiotics by day 4 in uncomplicated Enterobacterales bacteremia worked as well as later switching
articles.title: Early versus late transition to oral antibiotics in Enterobacterales bacteremia.
articles.population: 225 adults with uncomplicated Enterobacterales bacteremia, clinically stable within 72 hours with source control, 5 US hospitals
articles.summary: Patients switched to oral therapy by day 4 (133) were compared with those switched later (92). Treatment failure within 30 days (recurrence, escalation, infection-related readmission or death) was 6.0% vs 6.5%, with no significant difference. Early switching was linked to shorter median hospital stay (5 vs 7 days) and shorter total antibiotic courses (9 vs 12 days). Immunocompromised patients were excluded and the switch wasn't randomized.
articles.why: Adds to trial data supporting early oral step-down for gram-negative bacteremia from urinary or other controlled sources. Pharmacists can flag stable patients for a highly bioavailable oral agent (e.g., a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX when susceptible) once cultures return.

articles.takeaway: In sickle cell disease, DOACs prevented VTE recurrence as well as warfarin with about 75% less major bleeding
articles.title: Direct oral anticoagulants versus vitamin K antagonists for the treatment of venous thromboembolism in adults with sickle cell disease: a Bayesian meta-analysis.
articles.population: 4 retrospective studies, 271 adults with sickle cell disease and VTE (155 DOAC, 116 VKA)
articles.summary: Recurrent VTE didn't differ between DOACs and VKAs (OR 0.82, 95% credible interval 0.38–1.75), consistent with equipoise. Major bleeding was markedly lower with DOACs (OR 0.25, 95% CrI 0.07–0.80), with a 99% posterior probability that DOACs are safer. Heterogeneity was low, but all four studies were small and retrospective.
articles.why: Patients with sickle cell disease have frequent ED visits and high VTE rates. This supports a DOAC as a reasonable first choice at discharge, with attention to renal function, adherence and interactions.

articles.takeaway: Pharmacist review of patients going home on IV antibiotics improved regimen appropriateness but didn't shorten stays
articles.title: TOC-PAT: a novel approach to discharge stewardship.
articles.population: 267 adults discharged or planned for discharge on outpatient parenteral antibiotics (167 before, 100 after), 1 US community hospital
articles.summary: Stewardship pharmacists screened every patient headed home on IV antimicrobials and recommended changes. Median length of stay didn't change (9 vs 10 days), but appropriate regimens rose from 51.5% to 58%. Pharmacists made 68 interventions and teams accepted 66% of them, mostly changes in drug choice and IV-to-oral conversions.
articles.why: Discharge is a stewardship blind spot, and many OPAT regimens can be narrowed or switched to oral. It's a model for pharmacists at transitions of care, including ED patients sent home on daily IV antibiotics.

issues.note: A quiet Saturday window with no ED drug RCTs, so this issue runs short at 7 picks.
